Cryptomining 001 — a guided SOC investigation
  1 / 1
Start●

You have been handed six alerts. Work out what happened.

no experience needed

This is the alert your security team woke up to. Read it before you touch anything. It is not the only one — three different rules fired overnight and between them raised six alerts, all on the same server.

The alert your instructor was givenUnauthorized cryptomining on a server - service-account abuse, encoded downloader, recurring pool traffic. sec-win-05 : a service account (svc_backup) authenticated over the network. A few minutes later a PowerShell process with an encoded command argument was started, followed by a second, unfamiliar executable launched as that PowerShell process's child. The server then began making small, evenly spaced outbound connections on an unusual port to an external address it had just looked up in DNS.

Your job is to decide one thing: is this a real attack that must be escalated, or a false alarm that can be closed? You will answer it the way an analyst does — not by guessing, but by following the evidence from the very first search to the last and writing down what you find as you go. By the report card you will know the account, both programs, the pool, the port, and when each thing happened.

What this guide is

It starts at zeroNo security knowledge and no Elastic experience needed. The investigation itself is clicking and reading; the only typing is your report, at the end.
The pictures are realEvery screen picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, taken by screenshotting the real Kibana. Nothing is drawn from memory.
It never leaves you guessingAfter every step it says the exact number or text you should now be looking at, and a numbered circle points at the control.
It cleans up after itselfOne file starts the lab — setup-lab.cmd on Windows, setup-lab.sh on macOS or Linux — and one removes it completely.

How to move around

This guide is a deck of cards, one step each. Move through it however you like:

  • The Next and Back buttons at the bottom, or the arrow keys on your keyboard.
  • The row of pills under the header jumps you straight to any step.
  • On a phone, swipe left and right.
  • Press ? any time for help, or the printer icon to save the whole thing as a PDF. On the report card there is a second button that exports your submission as a PDF of its own.
Two honest notes, read these before you start

1. The pictures are real, which means you can see some of the answers. That is deliberate: the picture is the evidence, and the exercise is to run the query and read the value off your own screen before you look at ours. If you only read the pictures you will learn nothing, and the question you will be asked is whether you can find it unaided. A yellow box like this one is a slot for your answer, and there is deliberately no second colour anywhere in this guide — nothing here is filled in for you and no answer is printed inside it. Your instructor holds the key separately.

2. Kibana prints times in your computer’s timezone, and no setting changes that. The log records themselves are UTC. The pictures in this guide were taken on a machine set to UTC, so if yours is not, your clock times will differ from ours by that offset. The gaps between events are identical in every timezone — and every conclusion in this guide is built on gaps. Card 8 explains it properly.

The one thing you need first

Docker, installed and running — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux. That is the only prerequisite. The lab runs Elasticsearch and Kibana inside it and installs nothing else on your computer. If you do not have Docker yet, ask your instructor — this lab assumes it is already there.

Prep1

The words you need to know

read once

You will see all of these in the tool and in your report. Read them once now and the rest of the lab becomes much easier.

The pieces

AlertA rule that fires when something looks dangerous. It is a claim, not a fact. Your job is to decide whether it is true.
DiscoverThe Kibana screen where you type a search and read the matching log lines. You will spend all your time here.
Detection ruleThe logic behind an alert. It runs on a timer, queries your data and raises one alert per matching record. This lab ships you three of them, which between them raised six alerts.
ElasticsearchThe database that stores and searches the logs. Answers web addresses like localhost:9200.
KibanaThe website you do all the work in, sitting on top of Elasticsearch. Lives at localhost:5601.
IndexOne named pile of log records of the same shape. Ours are auth-* and network-*.
Data viewKibana’s word for “which pile shall I look at”. Older versions called it an index pattern.
DocumentOne single log record. There are 271 in the auth pile and 149 in the network pile. This is what you read.
FieldOne labelled box inside a document, like process.name. The part before the dot is the group.
TimestampThe @timestamp field — when it happened. All times in this lab are UTC.
QueryA typed question, like “show me events where the code is 4688”.
KQLThe query language Kibana speaks. The ? button in the search bar explains it.
IOCIndicator of Compromise — a piece of evidence that something bad happened: an address, a file name, a domain, an account.
Parent processThe program that started another program, recorded as process.parent.name. A child started by a downloader is a delivery chain.

The four that carry this whole investigation

Service accountAn account used by software, not a person — the names look like svc_backup. It should be driven by a scheduled job, not signed in to from somewhere. A service account in a logon you cannot explain is a finding in itself.
CryptominerA program that spends somebody else’s CPU and electricity mining cryptocurrency. It is quiet: nothing is encrypted, nothing looks broken, the server keeps answering normally.
Mining poolThe server the miner reports its hashes to. A miner always has to find one, which is why it makes a DNS lookup you can find in the logs.
Wallet addressThe “account number” the miner credits its earnings to. Miners are always told to put one on the command line, so it turns up in the process arguments — a very strong piece of evidence.
-EncodedCommandPowerShell’s way of taking a whole script as a base64 blob. Legitimate IT scripts use it; attackers use it so the real command is unreadable in the process list. On a server, an encoded PowerShell with a remote-execution parent is worth stopping for.
Remote-execution serviceA Windows service that lets something else tell a machine to run a program. wmiprvse.exe — the WMI provider host — is one. It is not a shell and not a desktop, so a process it started was started by something, from somewhere else.

The three fields that matter most

Almost every question in this investigation is answered by three fields. Learn these and the whole lab is just typing:

  • event.code — the number of the Windows log record. It tells you what kind of thing happened. You only need two of them:
    4688 = a process was created  ·  4624 = an account was successfully logged on
  • process.name and process.parent.name — on a 4688, what ran and what ran it. A child started by a downloader is a delivery chain, and reading it in order tells you how the attacker got there.
  • user.name — whose identity it ran as. A svc_… name is a service account: used by software rather than by a person.

Verdicts you will have to choose between

True positiveThe attack is real. Escalate it, contain it, tell someone.
False positiveNothing bad happened. Close the alert with a note saying why not.
The shape of the attack, before you see it

Cryptomining always has the same four beats: a service account is used to get in, something remote runs a PowerShell that fetches a file it will not let you read, that PowerShell starts the miner as its own child, and the miner resolves a stranger domain and then reports to it forever, in tiny, perfectly regular packets. Hold that pattern in your head. By the middle of this lab you will be hunting for it.

One practical note while you are here: numbers on screen are formatted with thousands separators. A process creation shows as 4,688, a port as 3,333, a byte count as 1,280. When you write them in your report, write the plain value (4688, 3333) so nobody reads 3,333 as a typo for 333.

Do this

  1. Open the lab folder — the folder that contains this guide.
  2. Find the setup file for your system and run it:
  3. On Windows: double-click setup-lab.cmd. A black command window opens and starts downloading Elasticsearch and Kibana. Do not close it.
  4. On macOS or Linux: open a terminal in that same folder and run ./setup-lab.sh. If your system says permission denied, run bash setup-lab.sh instead — that always works. To see what the file can do, run it with --help (a bare -? will not reach it: the shell swallows it first).

If the browser asks you to sign in

It will, because this lab’s Kibana has security switched on. A detection rule cannot be created against a cluster that has security off, so the lab turns it on. The account is lab_kibana and the password is LabKibana001. They are throwaway lab credentials that protect nothing, and you sign in once. The alert you are about to read is already waiting on the other side of that screen.

The one thing that stops most people

Docker must be installed and running. The lab runs both programs inside Docker containers. If the setup file says docker was not found, or that it is installed but not running, start it — Docker Desktop on Windows or macOS, Docker Engine on Linux — wait until it says it is running, then run the file again. That one check fixes almost every startup problem.

What you should see

A black window that works through numbered stages. It verifies its own work as it goes, so the last thing it prints before the addresses looks like this:

The end of the setup file's own verification every document in the auth data view = 271 every document in the network data view = 149 rule 1's own query, and so its alert = 1 rule 2's own query, and so its alert = 1 rule 3's own query, and so its alerts = 4 query 1 the estate's whole day = 21 query 2 the failed-logon dead end = 51 query 3 every powershell start = 5 query 4 the entry point = 1 query 5 the delivery chain = 2 query 6 the day's dns lookups = 32 query 7 the pool heartbeat = 4 [verify] every number the walkthrough quotes matches the live index.

Those seven numbers are the answers to this whole investigation. The script has already proved them against the live index, which is why you can trust every count in the rest of this guide. Then it prints:

The last thing setup-lab.cmd prints ============================================================ The lab is ready. Elasticsearch : http://127.0.0.1:9200 Kibana : http://127.0.0.1:5601 data view "auth" index pattern auth-* 271 documents data view "network" index pattern network-* 149 documents ============================================================

It also prints the seven investigation queries with the document count each one must return, so you have a reference sheet to check yourself against. If any of those counts disagrees with the data, the script says so and stops rather than hand you a lab that would mislead you.

What it did for you while you waited

  • Started two programs — Elasticsearch (the database) and Kibana (the website) — inside containers whose names all begin with this folder’s own name.
  • Taught Elasticsearch what each field means. An index template declares “source.ip holds a network address” before any data arrives. Without it Elasticsearch guesses, and guessing quietly breaks your searches.
  • Loaded 271 + 149 log records. If it had already loaded them it says so and imports nothing — your data cannot load twice, which matters because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide.
  • Created your two data views and then read them back to prove the index pattern really was stored. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing at all, and the cause of that is invisible, so the script checks it instead of hoping.
  • Installed the three detection rules and waited for all three to fire. The alerts you are about to read did not exist until the script did that, and the script does not print ready until all six are really there. If a rule had matched nothing you would have been told so instead of being handed an empty page.

Already started it twice?

Completely safe. The script counts what is already loaded and skips it. Your data will not load twice — which matters, because duplicate documents would double every count in the rest of this guide and ruin your findings. If it ever finds a half-loaded dataset it refuses to add to it and tells you to run the setup file with reset instead.

What you are looking at

Do this

  1. Read Alerts by name and write down all three rule names exactly, with the count beside each: 4, 1, 1.
  2. Read Severity levels: Critical 1, High 5, total 6. Write the total down. The report asks for it.
  3. Read the Risk Score column. Two rules score 73 and one scores 99. Notice which rule is the 99: it is the one that names the miner.

  5. Open an alert. In the first column, called Actions, click the first small icon on the top row — the two arrows pointing outwards.

What one alert says

This lab is generous, and that is deliberate

Be clear-eyed about what you have just been given. The miner rule literally says xmrig.exe. The network rule’s reason literally says 198.51.100.77:3333. You did not work those out; a rule did, and it printed them in a sentence.

That is a real trade-off, and real SOCs make it constantly. A rule that names the miner binary is easy to write and catches the miner. A rule that names a port catches the beacon. The cost is that a rule is a claim, not a finding — it can be wrong, it can be matched by something innocent, and on its own it proves nothing about what came before it or what the attacker got.

So the rest of this lab is not about finding out that a miner ran. It already told you. It is about proving the chain — that this server, this service account, this PowerShell, this child process and these four connections are one incident, in that order, on one morning — and about deciding how bad it was. That is the part a rule cannot do for you.

All six, so you can see it is one incident

Read this table off the page. The original time column is the attack, not the alert; the next box explains where it comes from. Times are UTC, and Kibana shows them in your own computer’s timezone, so read the gaps rather than the absolute numbers.

Rule Severity Risk Original time (UTC) What it matched
PowerShell started by a remote-execution servicehigh7309:43:00powershell.exe whose parent was wmiprvse.exe
Known cryptominer binary started on a servercritical9909:45:00xmrig.exe, two minutes later
Tiny outbound keepalives on a single non-standard porthigh7309:46:001280 bytes to 198.51.100.77:3333
Tiny outbound keepalives on a single non-standard porthigh7309:51:001536 bytes to 198.51.100.77:3333
Tiny outbound keepalives on a single non-standard porthigh7309:56:001024 bytes to 198.51.100.77:3333
Tiny outbound keepalives on a single non-standard porthigh7310:01:001408 bytes to 198.51.100.77:3333

Eighteen minutes from the first alert to the last, one host, one user, three rules. Four identical-looking alerts are not four problems. They are one ongoing conversation with a mining pool, and a report that lists six separate findings has missed the point entirely.

Two different times, and the difference matters

The alert’s own timestamp is when the rule ran. The log record underneath it happened on 22 September, between 09:43 and 10:01 UTC, which is the morning of the attack. So the alerts are new and the events they point at are old, and the alerts page will keep showing them while Discover, which looks at the events themselves, shows you nothing at all until you set its time range. That is the next card, and it is not a fault.

You are not imagining it, and nothing has gone wrong. Click the JSON tab in the alert panel and you will find two clocks on it:

The two timestamps, from this lab's first alert@timestamp 2026-09-30T04:53:00.342Z the day YOU ran this kibana.alert.original_time 2026-09-22T09:43:00.000Z the morning of the attack

@timestamp is when Elastic noticed. It is the day you ran the setup file, so it is a different date for every batch and it tells you nothing about the attack — yours will not be the date above. kibana.alert.original_time is when the activity actually happened, and that one never moves — for this lab it is always 22 September.

Every real SOC works this way, because logs often arrive late or a rule is run against history, and if alerts were dated by the event then today’s real alerts would be buried under a wall of old ones. Which one goes in your report? The original time. Every time you write in this lab, write the time of the activity, never the time the tool noticed it.

The three rules that fired

Worth seeing, because each rule is a filter — and each one is narrower than the story it sits inside.

  1. Close the alert panel with the × at the top right, then click Rules in the Security menu on the left. Older builds call the page Detection rules.
  2. You should see three rules, all of them custom, all switched on. Click any one of them and read its Custom query in the Definition box on the right.
# Rule Alerts Custom query
1PowerShell started by a remote-execution service1event.code: 4688 and process.name: "powershell.exe" and process.parent.name: "wmiprvse.exe"
2Known cryptominer binary started on a server1event.code: 4688 and process.name: "xmrig.exe"
3Tiny outbound keepalives on a single non-standard port4event.action: "network_connection" and destination.port: 3333 and network.bytes < 2048

Read rule 3 carefully, because the shape of it is the lesson. It does not say “this is a mining pool”. It says: a connection, to one port, carrying fewer than two kilobytes. That is a volume test, and cryptomining is the textbook case where a volume test beats a name test — because the miner sends almost nothing, on purpose, forever.

Why the rules stop where they stop

Each one is a single filter over a single index, and each one is blind to something the others can see. Rule 1 watches auth-* and knows nothing about DNS or outbound traffic. Rule 3 watches network-* and cannot see a process name at all — which is why the network records you are about to query have no process.name on them, and why you have to join the two halves yourself.

Between them they have told you that a service account was abused, that a miner binary ran, and that something was beaconing. What they have not told you is that the PowerShell was encoded, that it was the miner’s parent, that the pool’s name was resolved by DNS a minute before the first connection, that the four connections are five minutes apart and almost exactly the same size, and that all of it was one host, one user, eighteen minutes.

Those are your job, and they are what turns a rule’s 73 and 99 into a justified severity in a report. If you agree the rules fired correctly, say so and move on; if you think one fired correctly but its severity is too low or too high, say that too, with a reason. That sentence is one of the few things that separates an analyst from someone who clicked through an alert queue.

If the table is empty, it is the time picker

Not a broken lab. An alert is stamped with the time it was raised, so the range this page starts on — Today, meaning from midnight — stops covering it once you cross midnight. Click the time picker at the top right, switch to the Relative tab, and set it to 1 unit Days. The alerts come straight back. Some versions put a ready-made Last 24 hours button there instead, which does the same job. The lab itself never changed.

What you should have now

Three rules, six alerts, one critical and five high, risk scores 73, 73 and 99, every one of them against a process or a connection on sec-win-05 running as svc_backup. The four network alerts name a pool at 198.51.100.77:3333 and arrived five minutes apart between 09:46 and 10:01 UTC. The process alerts name powershell.exe under wmiprvse.exe and then xmrig.exe under that PowerShell.

You have not run a single query yet, and you already have the shape of the attack handed to you. What you do not have is the evidence — the encoded command, the parent relationship proven from the logs, the DNS name, and the proof that the four connections are one long conversation rather than four coincidences. That is the next fifteen cards.

Your browser just opened. Here is where you are.

no typing needed

You have read the alert. Now come to Discover, where the investigation happens — click the hamburger menu (☰) in the top left and then Discover. This card exists because this screen looks broken, and it is not — it is simply showing you nothing yet, because the attack is a week old and Discover is looking at the last few minutes. Let’s read it together, piece by piece.

Do this

  1. Click the blue Search entire time range button in the middle of the screen. That is it — one click and your records appear.
  2. Check the Data view control on the far left says auth-*. It does, and that is the one you want.

Here is the screen before you click. Every word, button and number in this picture is the real Kibana 9.1.0 interface, and the numbered circles are pinned to the exact controls they describe.

So what is wrong right now?

Exactly one thing: the time range. The data view is right, the search bar is right, Kibana is healthy. The records are simply older than the last fifteen minutes.

That is the single most common reason a beginner meets an empty screen. The Search entire time range button fixes it for you. The next card shows you how to do the same thing by hand, so you can pin an exact window rather than “everything”.

One button on that toolbar you must ignore

Next to Inspect and Alerts there is a white button called Try ES|QL. ES|QL is a different query language, advertised to people who already know their way around Kibana. Card 16 shows you exactly what it does to your results if you click it. For this whole lab, use only the KQL search bar.

Pick a pile5

Choose which pile of logs to look at

which logs?2 min

First, tell Discover which pile of logs to read. You have two, and only one of them is where this attack starts.

Do this

  1. Click the control on the far left of the search bar row — the box with the label Data view beside it. It currently reads auth-*.
  2. Look at the list that opens. It has three entries and one heading: All logs, then the heading Managed, then auth-* and network-*. Leave auth-* selected — that is the one you want for the next four queries, so if it already has a tick there is nothing to do.

What the two data views are

Data viewHoldsRecordsFields
auth-*Successful and failed logons, logoffs, privilege changes, account lockouts, Kerberos failures, and process creations27118
network-*Connections (SMB, RPC, LDAP, HTTP/HTTPS, SSH, ICMP) and DNS lookups with their answers14922
Why this matters

A data view is a bookmark. It tells Kibana which pile of documents to read and which field holds the time. Pick the wrong one and a perfectly good query returns nothing at all, because the documents it is looking for are not in that pile.

So whenever a query returns zero results, check these three things in this order: the data view, then the time range, then the query itself. Nine times out of ten it is one of the first two, never the third.

If the dropdown is empty, or the sidebar says “no fields” even after you pick one

Then the data views were not created properly. Do not fight it — run setup-lab.cmd again. It is safe to run twice, it reloads nothing, and it now reads each data view back after creating it and tells you if the index pattern did not stick, instead of printing a hopeful message. A data view with an empty pattern matches nothing, and Discover then shows zero fields and no results with no clue why.

Be precise6

Set the time range to the right day

pin an exact window3 min

Your data is loaded and the right data view is selected. The screen is still empty for one reason only, and this card fixes it for good.

Do this

  1. Click the time control on the right of the search bar row. It reads Last 15 minutes. A little panel opens with a list of quick choices.
  2. Inside that panel, click the left-most of the three tabs. There are three, and in this version Absolute is the first one, then Relative, then Now. You want Absolute, because that lets you type a real date.
  3. A calendar appears with a field at the bottom labelled Start date, and End date just below it. Click into Start date, select what is there, and type Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000
  4. Click into End date and type Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999.
  5. Close the panel. The control in the search bar now shows both dates and the results reload on their own. There is no separate Apply button to hunt for in this version.
The one thing that will look “wrong”: Kibana prints times in your timezone

This trips up almost everyone, so read it before you go further.

The timestamps in this lab are stored in UTC. But the @timestamp column, the histogram axis, and the friendly dates inside a document all follow your computer’s timezone, and nothing in the time picker changes that. If your machine is 8 hours ahead of UTC, the logon this guide calls 09:40:00.000 appears in your table as 17:40:00.000.

So which is right? Both, and it does not matter. Here is the rule that keeps you out of trouble:

  • Read the clock times off your own screen and write down what you see. Your timeline will be internally consistent, which is all a timeline needs.
  • Trust the gaps, not the absolute numbers. Every conclusion in this guide is about how far apart things are, and a timezone shift moves every time by the same amount. The gaps — 3 minutes, then 2, then 0, then 1, then 5, 5, 5 — are identical in every timezone.
  • If you want the screen to match this guide exactly, set your computer’s timezone to UTC before you start. Not required — but then nothing on the following cards will look out of place. The pictures in this guide were all taken with the machine set to UTC.

What you should see now

The time control reads Sep 22, 2026 @ 00:00:00.000 → Sep 22, 2026 @ 23:59:59.999 and, for the first time, your records are there.

What each part of that screen is, because you will look at it six more times
  • The row across the top picks which pile (Data view), lets you type what to look for (the search bar), and picks when (the time control).
  • The sidebar on the left lists the fields that exist, grouped as Selected fields, Popular fields and Available fields. Hovering a field gives you a small + that adds it as a column, and Add a field at the very bottom does the same from a searchable list. That is how you widen the table in the cards below.
  • The histogram shows how many records fall in each half hour. A gap in the bars means nothing happened then.
  • The table below is the records themselves. The summary column shows every field of a record at once, which is why the later cards ask you to add specific columns rather than read that wall of text.
Remember this one, and it will save you hours

An empty screen in Kibana is almost never a broken query. It is almost always the time range or the data view. Check those two first, every time.

And beware: if you press F5 to reload, or wander off to another Kibana page and come back, the time range can snap back to Last 15 minutes and the screen goes empty again. That is not your fault and it is not broken — just repeat this card. Keeping the working Discover tab in a bookmark is what experienced analysts do for exactly this reason.

Investigate7

Query 1 — the baseline: every program that started

1 of 7 queries2 min
Goal of this step

Find out what a normal day on this estate looks like, so that later a number which does not fit stands out. Also: learn the one query you will use more than any other.

Do this

  1. Make sure the data view still says auth-* and the time range is still the whole of 22 September 2026.
  2. Click into the search bar, clear it, and type the query below. Then press Enter.
Query 1 — data view auth-* event.code: 4688

What the query means, clause by clause

  • event.code is the number Windows gives to a type of log record. In this lab the field is event.code, not event.id, so if you are used to another tool this is the one thing to check.
  • 4688 means “a new process has been created”. Every time anything at all starts on a Windows machine, one of these is written. It is your window into what actually ran.
  • No other filter, on purpose. We are taking the whole estate, not one server, so that we can see what ordinary looks like.

What you should see

The tab reads Documents (21). Write that number down — it is your control figure. Then widen the table: hover a field name in the left sidebar and click the small + beside it, or use the Columns button above the table. The five columns below are what you want.

What you have just established

On an ordinary day this estate starts 21 programs across four servers (sec-win-01, -02, -04, -05) as six different people. The programs are ordinary too: msedge.exe, notepad.exe, regedit.exe, taskmgr.exe, wmic.exe, cmd.exe, powershell.exe.

Two things are now on your list. Only one server has just three records in the whole pile, and only one of the six accounts appears three times in total. Both turn out to matter. Hold on to the number 21.

Next

The obvious next move for almost any alert is to look at failed logons. Card 9 does exactly that, and it is a dead end. Doing the obvious thing and understanding why it fails is the point of the next card.

Wrong turn8

Query 2 — failed logons. This one is a dead end.

dead end — on purpose3 min
Goal of this step

Take the first obvious action — search for failed logons — and learn exactly why it proves nothing here. Doing this and understanding why it fails is worth more than skipping it.

Do this

  1. In the search bar, clear the old query and type the one below. Press Enter.
  2. Read the number in the Documents tab, then read the user.name column.
Query 2 — data view auth-* event.code: 4625

4625 means “an account failed to log on”. It is the record you would look at in a password-guessing investigation, so it is the first thing anyone types.

What you should see

Documents (51). Fifty-one failed logons. That is a big, alarming number, and it is exactly the number of rows in the table below it — you can count them.

Stop. This number means nothing here, and that is the lesson.

Break the 51 down before you go anywhere near it. These are the real figures, and you can get every one of them yourself by clicking a single value in the table:

  • They belong to five different accounts: rneuman 16, kpatel 13, asmith 8, jdoe 7, mchen 7.
  • They are on three different servers: sec-win-04 23, sec-win-01 14, sec-win-02 14.
  • None of them is the service account in the alert, and none of them is on the server in the alert.
  • They are spread across the whole day, not clustered into a burst.

People mistype passwords. Laptops sleep and wake on a VPN. A service account with a saved password on a desktop that reboots will generate a handful of these a week forever. 51 failures across 5 people and 3 servers over 24 hours is a completely ordinary day.

It is a pattern that would be evidence: forty failures in four minutes from one address against one account is an attack. A raw total is not.

Why this matters more than the next four cards

Every real investigation is a sequence of queries, and most of them return nothing. The skill is not typing the right query first time — it is recognising quickly that a number is ordinary and moving on, instead of building a story on it.

Write this down as the rule for the rest of the lab: a count is not a finding until you know what it is a count of.

Next

Second obvious move: “it mentions PowerShell, let me search for PowerShell.” Card 10 does that — and it is a better trap than this one, because the number it gives you is a real 5, not zero.

Wrong turn9

Query 3 — every PowerShell start, before you narrow it

5 hits, only 1 matters3 min
Goal of this step

Search for the thing the alert named, on purpose without narrowing to the server. Then see why “narrow first” is the rule, and not “narrow later”.

Do this

  1. Clear the search bar and type the query below. Press Enter.
  2. Add host.name and process.parent.name as columns if they are not there already.
  3. Read all five rows, and read the parent column, not the name column.
Query 3 — data view auth-* event.code: 4688 and process.name: "powershell.exe"

The double quotes matter. Without them Kibana splits the value at the dot and you get a different, wrong result. Every value in this guide that contains a dot or a dash is quoted, so you can copy it exactly.

What you should see

Documents (5). Five PowerShell processes. Now read the parent column of each one. Four of them say explorer.exe. One says something else.

Why “narrow first” beats “narrow later”

Search for powershell.exe across the estate and you get 5. The answer you want is 1. Four fifths of that result set is a person opening a script, and it is pure noise for this investigation.

That matters more than tidiness. If you had been handed the five rows in a ticket, you would have had to argue about each one. If you had been handed the alert’s server first, you would have had one row and no argument at all. Every filter you can apply from facts you already have is a filter that removes work, not adds it.

You already had that server name in the alert text. You should have used it in the first query.

The other thing this table teaches, and it is the whole case

Look at that bottom row again. Its process.parent.name is wmiprvse.exe. That is not a shell and not a desktop. It is the Windows Management Instrumentation provider host — a remote execution service. It means the PowerShell was not started by a person sitting at the machine. Something was told to run it, from somewhere else.

So the same five-row table has already given you the shape of the whole incident: a service account did not sign in to the machine, something remote started a PowerShell, and no human was involved. Note that this conclusion came from the parent column, which is why the cards keep telling you to add it.

Next

Card 11 does the query properly: the same search, narrowed to the one server in the alert. That is the one that closes the entry point.

Entry point10

Query 4 — the logon that started it

4 of 7 queries4 min
Goal of this step

Prove the alert’s first claim and turn it into evidence. An alert says a service account signed in over the network; a finding shows the record and explains why it is not normal.

Do this

  1. Clear the search bar and type the query below. Press Enter.
  2. The tab should read Documents (1). One row.
  3. Open the row. Do not click the row itself — in Discover, clicking a row does nothing at all. Click the small button made of two diagonal arrows, immediately to the left of the timestamp. That opens the record on the right and shows every field with its type.
Query 4 — data view auth-* event.code: 4624 and user.name: "svc_backup" and host.name: "sec-win-05"

Clause by clause: event.code: 4624 keeps only successful logons; user.name is the account the alert named; host.name is the server the alert named; and means all three must be true. All three values came from the alert, not from the data — you are not guessing, you are confirming.

What you should see

Documents (1), and one row.

And here is that one record, opened:

Write these four into your timeline now
  • The account: the service account from the alert — and notice it appears only 3 times in the whole 271-record pile, all of them on this one server.
  • The logon type: 3, a network logon.
  • The server’s own address, from host.ip.
  • The address it came from, from source.ip, and the timestamp.
Read the message field too — it is the analyst’s best friend

Scroll down in that panel to message. These records spell out in plain English what each one is, including the logon type and the source address. Real log records very often carry a human-readable summary like this, and reading it is much faster than assembling the story from fields.

It is not a substitute for the fields — a message can be truncated or simply wrong — but it is a very good place to start, and it is the first thing an experienced analyst looks at.

Why this matters

You cannot call something an incident until you know how the attacker got in. A service account is the classic weak link: long-lived, shared, often privileged, and its logons are so routine that nobody watches them. Nobody signs into a service account with a password — software does, from wherever it happens to be running. So a type-3 logon by a service account is either a scheduled job, or something using that account as a key. This logon is the entry point, and every later step is a consequence of it.

Delivery11

Query 5 — the two programs on the victim server

5 of 7 queries6 min
Goal of this step

Find what the attacker actually ran, and prove the order it ran in. This result set is the entire infection on the host.

Do this

  1. Clear the search bar and type the query below. Press Enter.
  2. Add process.name, process.parent.name, user.name and process.command_line as columns, and keep @timestamp sorted oldest first.
  3. The tab should read Documents (2). Write the number down, then read both rows in time order.
Query 5 — data view auth-*  ·  this is also the single one-shot query in the companion brief event.code: 4688 and host.name: "sec-win-05"

Notice what is not in this query. It does not name the suspicious program, and it does not name any domain. Both are things you are supposed to discover, so naming them would hand you the answer. It asks only two questions: a process started, and it was on the server in the alert.

What you should see

Documents (2). Two programs. On a busy server you would expect hundreds or thousands of these; two is itself unusual, and worth noticing.

Read the first record properly

Open it in the Document panel. If the value is too long to read on one line, click the small ⊕ button beside the field name — that expands it in place instead of scrolling sideways.

Then prove it with the Field statistics tab

One click, and it summarises the result set instead of listing it. Click Field statistics — the tab immediately to the right of Documents (2):

The chain so far, in order
  • A service account signed in over the network to the server in the alert. (card 11)
  • Three minutes later a PowerShell with an encoded payload was started by a remote-execution service, not by a person. (this card)
  • Two minutes after that an unfamiliar program was started by that PowerShell, as the same service account, with a pool host and a wallet in its arguments.

That is a coherent, ordered chain, and you built it out of two rows. One query per clause of your verdict is how an analyst makes a conclusion arguable rather than merely plausible.

Next

A miner cannot talk to a pool until it resolves the pool’s name, and DNS lookups are logged. Card 13 switches to the other data view and finds the stranger domain — which is how you turn a name in a command line into an address you can block.

The join12

Query 6 — the DNS lookup that gave it away

6 of 7 queries4 min
Goal of this step

Card 12 gave you a name in a command line. Names cannot be blocked, counted or chased — but addresses can. This step turns the name into an address.

Do this

  1. Switch the Data view to network-*. Same control, top left; it now has a tick beside it. The sidebar field list changes completely — that is correct, it is a different pile of records.
  2. Keep the time range. It carries over.
  3. Clear the search bar, type the query below, press Enter.
  4. Add source.ip, dns.question.name, dns.resolved_ip and dns.response_code as columns.
Query 6 — data view network-* event.action: "dns_query"

event.action is the same information as event.code but in plain words instead of a number. In this pile the four values are dns_query (a lookup), network_connection (a connection), connection_refused and connection_terminated. When a number and a word describe the same event, prefer the word — you can read it.

What you should see

Documents (32). Thirty-two lookups — a few dozen, an ordinary day’s worth. Write the number down, then read the dns.question.name column from top to bottom.

How to spot the one, without reading 32 rows carefully
  1. Read the source.ip column and look for the server you have been chasing. The only lookup from that server’s own address is the odd one. This takes five seconds and it is the fastest method on this card.
  2. Click any value in a column to filter the whole table down to just those rows. Click NOERROR and you lose the three that did not resolve. Click a single address and you lose everything that host did not ask for. Clicking a value is the same as writing a new query, and it is how experienced analysts explore.
  3. Only then read the names. Almost all of them are suppliers or your own internal domain. One is a stranger.

Write down the name and the address from that row. Both. You need the address in the next card, and the name is a high-value indicator you can block at the resolver and hunt across the whole estate.

Three lookups in that list failed. Is that a problem?

No. Three rows have dns.response_code of NXDOMAIN and an empty dns.resolved_ip: the name did not exist. A machine asked for something that is not there, the resolver said so, and the machine moved on. That happens constantly — typos, software phoning home to a retired service, ad blockers rewriting names.

An empty cell is not a broken lab. It is the answer to a question you did not know you were asking. The suspicious lookup is the opposite: it resolved successfully, to an external address, from a server that has no business knowing it.

Why this card is the most important one in the deck

It is the join between the two data views. auth-* gave you a name in a command line. network-* gives you the address that name points at. You cannot count sessions to a name, you cannot block a name at your firewall, and you cannot search last month’s traffic for it either. The moment you have the pair, you can do all three.

Note also what the timestamps say. This lookup is at the same instant as the miner starting — the program looked its pool up before it did anything else. That is the ordering of a working attack, not a coincidence.

Proof13

Query 7 — the heartbeat to the pool

7 of 7 queries4 min
Goal of this step

Count the sessions to that address, and prove they are a machine-paced heartbeat. This is the step that turns “a program with a suspicious name” into “an ongoing, monetised operation”.

Do this

  1. Stay on network-*. Clear the search bar, type the query below, press Enter.
  2. Use your own values. The two addresses and the port in this query are the ones this dataset produces. If you read different ones in cards 10 and 12, type yours — that is the entire point of doing those steps first.
  3. Add source.port and network.bytes as columns.
Query 7 — data view network-* source.ip: "10.0.4.30" and destination.ip: "198.51.100.77" and destination.port: 3333

Clause by clause: source.ip is traffic leaving the compromised server — the address you wrote down from host.ip in card 11. destination.ip is the address the stranger name resolved to, from card 13. destination.port is the unusual port from the miner’s arguments. All three literals came from your own earlier results, not from me.

What you should see

Documents (4). Four sessions. Now do not read the byte column and conclude “that is nothing”. Read the times.

The trap on this card: the bytes are tiny, and that is not the point

Look at network.bytes. The four sessions are 1,280, 1,536, 1,024 and 1,408 bytes — about five kilobytes in total. A colleague glancing at that would say “that cannot be an attack, it is nothing”.

They would be wrong, and this is the most common way a cryptomining investigation gets closed when it should be escalated. Mining traffic is not a download. The binary arrives once, in a single burst you may never see on this host, and after that the miner sends tiny packets of work to the pool and gets tiny shares back, forever. The volume is small by design. A miner that moved gigabytes would be a miner somebody noticed.

So judge this traffic on four things, none of which is size:

  • Regularity. The same gap, over and over, to the second. Machines repeat; people do not.
  • The port. Not 80, not 443. A fixed, unusual number belonging to a protocol rather than a website.
  • Who it is going to. An external address your servers have no business talking to, resolved from a domain that appeared in a process argument which also named a wallet.
  • What came before it. These four sessions sit after the logon and after the two programs. Timeline order is evidence; coincidence is not.

Read one session in full

Open the first row with the two-diagonal-arrow button, as in card 11:

You now have a verdict

Not because one number was big, but because five independent facts agree, each from a different kind of record:

  • A service account signed in over the network to a server it should only be used on by a scheduled job.
  • Three minutes later, a PowerShell with an encoded payload was started by a remote-execution service — not by a person.
  • Two minutes after that, an unfamiliar program was started by that PowerShell, as the same account, naming a pool and a wallet in its arguments.
  • The server then resolved a stranger domain that nothing else in the estate had ever asked for.
  • And it then held four tiny, perfectly five-minute-spaced sessions to that address, on a non-standard port, from one fixed source port.

That is a coherent chain, every link of it timestamped, every link of it in a record you can point at. Verdict: true positive. You do not need one more query to be sure, and you should not go hunting for a bigger number to be more sure — the evidence is already complete.

Trap14

Do not read your count off the Try ES|QL screen

a real trap, no error1 min

One card about a button you were told to ignore, because it fails quietly rather than loudly — which is worse.

What happens

On the toolbar, next to Inspect and Alerts, there is a white button called Try ES|QL. Click it and Discover changes into a different query language. It works — nothing breaks and no error appears — and that is exactly why it is dangerous.

The rule this teaches

Always read the count from the same screen you read the rows from, and know which screen that is. A number produced by a different tool, a different view or a different limit is not a smaller problem to check later — it is a different number, and it will not match anything you find when you verify.

For this lab: the number to trust is the one inside the Documents (N) tab in the classic Discover screen. Write that number down every single time, and if you ever write a number from anywhere else, say so in your report.

Coming back

Click Switch to classic at the top left and you are back in the screen this guide uses. Nothing is lost — your query is still there and the time range is unchanged. Or press the browser’s Back button a couple of times.

Put it together15

Build the timeline

oldest first5 min

Open a blank note — paper, a text file, anything — and turn your findings into one ordered list, oldest first, with the times you read off your own screen.

Six rows, and a gap column

  1. Make a table with three columns: Time, Gap, What happened.
  2. Fill in one row per stage, using the times from cards 10 to 13.
  3. The Gap column is the one that makes the pattern obvious, and it is the only column that is identical in every timezone. Compute it: subtract each time from the one above it.
Time you readGapWhat happened — and where you proved it
your screen — A service account signed in over the network to the server in the alert, from an internal address that is not the server itself. Logon type your answer. (Query 4, and the Document panel.)
your screen 3 min A PowerShell with an -EncodedCommand value started, with a remote-execution service as its parent — not a person. (Query 5, row 1.)
your screen 2 min An unfamiliar program started as that PowerShell’s own child, as the same account, with a pool host and a wallet in its arguments. (Query 5, row 2.)
your screen 0 min The server resolved a stranger domain — the same instant, because a miner looks its pool up before it does anything else. (Query 6.)
your screen 1 min First session to that address, on a non-standard port. (Query 7.)
your screen then 5, 5, 5 Three more sessions — same gap each time, same source port, kilobytes each. Total: how many? (Query 7.)
What your timeline should tell you, in one line

Somebody signed in, fetched a program, ran it, found a pool, and started reporting to it — all inside about twenty minutes, all as the same service account, all on one server.

Twenty minutes is itself the finding. A compromise that completes in twenty minutes is automated: this was a script, not a person at a keyboard. Say that in your report. It changes how urgently anyone has to act.

Why the gap column is the important one

Because of the timezone problem in card 7. Absolute clock times move depending on where you are sitting; gaps do not move at all. The three-minute gap to the downloader, the two-minute gap to the miner, the five-minute heartbeat — those are facts about the attacker’s behaviour, and they are true on every machine in the world.

So when you write your report, give the gaps as your primary evidence and the absolute times as your reference, and label the times UTC. That is what makes your timeline checkable by someone sitting on the other side of the planet.

Do not skip this card

It is the card that feels like paperwork, and it is the one that turns a pile of queries into a finding. An on-call engineer will read your timeline first and decide within thirty seconds whether to wake somebody up. If your timeline is a list of queries instead of a list of events, they cannot do that.

Deliverable16

Write the report, then prove it

25 mindo not skip

Nobody reads your screen. This card is the deliverable — it is the thing you hand in, and it is the only place in the guide you type. It has two parts and both go into your submission: Part one is your written report, Part two is the set of figures you checked off your own screen as you went. Neither part has an answer printed next to it. Fill both in, then press EXPORT MY SUBMISSION at the bottom: a finished PDF report lands in your Downloads folder with your name and batch number on the front of it.

Do this yourself, and do it now

If you cannot fill a line in without going back to Kibana, you have not finished the investigation — which is exactly the point. These fields are deliberately empty and stay that way until you type. Nothing here is marked against a model answer; it is marked on whether you found these things.

Both of these are printed at the top of the exported PDF and go into the file name, so the submission is identifiable without you having to say who you are in the report itself. Leave either one blank and the file still exports — it just says [not answered] where your name should be, which is a good reason not to leave them blank.

Part one — your report

1. Summary

What happened

two or three sentences a manager could follow, and no jargon in the first sentence

2. Timeline

When

one line per stage, oldest first, with the times read off your own screen — not off this guide — and the gap since the line above it

3. Evidence

How you know

each query you ran, the number it returned, and what that number proved. The number matters as much as the reasoning — and record the queries that proved nothing, too

4. Verdict

True positive or false positive

state it plainly in the first line, then the whole chain in one paragraph, and say whether you agree with the rule's severity of high / 73

5. Recommendations

What should happen next

concrete actions in the order you would carry them out: contain, then credential, then block, then hunt. If something has to be done twice to actually work, say so

Part two — the figures behind it

Every line below is a number you should be able to point at on your own screen. These travel with your report, so a figure that contradicts your writing gives you away — if Part one and Part two disagree, one of them is wrong, and you want to know which before you hand it in.

Your verdict in one line

Two things worth double-checking in your own report

These are the two that catch people out, so read yours back now:

  1. Did you count the pool sessions, or dismiss them for being small? Four sessions totalling about five kilobytes is the whole of the mining traffic in this lab. Mining is a heartbeat, not a download — a report that says “the byte volume was negligible, so this is not an attack” has closed a live incident. The evidence is the regularity, the fixed source port and the stranger destination, never the size.
  2. Did you use your own values in Query 7? If you typed the address and port straight out of this guide instead of reading them off your own Query 6, the number you get back is not a finding — it is a number the guide gave you. The guide told you to use your own on purpose.

And one bonus: if you read process.command_line closely enough to notice the -EncodedCommand value, say so in your report. It is not required and nothing checks it automatically, but it is the sentence that turns a list of counts into a story — it is the difference between “a program called xmrig.exe exists” and “someone remote made this server fetch a file it could not read, and run it.”

Export it

Anything you left blank is written in as [not answered] rather than quietly dropped, so a hole cannot turn into a tidy-looking submission. The PDF lands in your Downloads folder; nothing is uploaded and no internet connection is needed.

Clean up17

Tear the lab down

leave no trace1 min

Finished. Now remove the lab completely. This matters: the lab stores its data in a Docker volume, and volumes are not removed when you close a window or shut down your computer. Left behind, they silently occupy disk space until somebody deletes them by hand.

Do this

  1. Make sure you have submitted your report. The teardown deletes the data.
  2. Close your browser and every Kibana tab.
  3. In the lab folder, run the teardown file for your system: on Windows, double-click teardown.cmd; on macOS or Linux, run ./teardown.sh in a terminal in that folder (or bash teardown.sh).
  4. It prints the exact list of what it is about to remove, and asks you to confirm (Y or N on Windows, y or n on macOS and Linux). Read the list, then say yes.
  5. It finishes by verifying the removal and telling you what was kept.

What it deletes — and what it does not

ObjectNameWhy
Containercryptomining-001-elasticsearchThe database process
Containercryptomining-001-kibanaThe website process
Networkcryptomining-001_defaultThe private network they shared
Volumecryptomining-001_esdataAll 420 log records — the disk space
Folderelklab-cryptomining-001Temporary files the setup made, in your temp directory
Filedocker-compose.ymlRegenerated by setup each time
What it deliberately keeps
  • The Elasticsearch and Kibana images. These are the big downloads — over a gigabyte together. Keeping them means the next time you run this lab, the setup file starts in seconds instead of twenty minutes. It never removes an image and never runs docker system prune.
  • Every other container and volume on this machine, so a second lab running beside this one is safe.
  • Your files. The log data, the templates and this guide are all still in the folder afterwards.

Every object name above begins with this lab’s own folder name. That is not a coincidence — it is how the script guarantees it can only ever delete its own lab, and nothing else on your machine.

What you should see

The end of what the teardown file prints ============================================================== The "cryptomining-001" lab has been removed. Kept on purpose: every Docker image, and every other container and volume on this machine. The log files and templates in this folder are also untouched, so nothing was lost from disk here. To build the lab again from scratch : setup-lab.cmd ==============================================================

Yours will name teardown.cmd or teardown.sh at the end depending on your system, and it prints a Verifying… block first, one line per object, saying gone or absent for each. Absent means there was nothing to remove, which is what a second run correctly reports.

Running teardown twice is harmless

It checks what is actually there first, tells you there is nothing to do, and exits. It will not complain, and it will not go looking for something else to clean up. That matters, because people run it twice to be sure.

You can also check it yourself: there should be no cryptomining-001_esdata entry under Volumes in Docker Desktop, and neither container should be in Containers. The script verifies this itself and warns you if anything is left behind.

Why bother?

Two reasons, and the second is the important one.

Practical: a lab volume is real disk space, and a machine with a dozen abandoned lab volumes will eventually run out of room or fail to start new containers. Cleaning up is part of being a professional.

Discipline: an analyst who leaves environments running on a shared or corporate machine causes real problems — port conflicts, somebody else’s lab failing to start, resources nobody knows are being used. Leave it as you found it is a habit worth forming now, before anybody is paying you for it.

Would rather just stop it and keep the data?

Sometimes you want the lab back tomorrow without waiting for it to reload. Run docker compose -f docker-compose.yml down in a terminal in the lab folder and the containers stop but everything is kept, because the data lives in the Docker volume. Bring it all back with docker compose -f docker-compose.yml up -d, or simply run the setup file again — it is safe to run twice and will not re-import anything.

Reference⚙

If something goes wrong

keep this open

Almost every problem in this lab is one of four things. Check them in this order before assuming the worst.

A query returns nothing

  • Check the time range. This is the cause nine times out of ten. It should show both dates of 22 September 2026. Reloading the page, or coming back from another Kibana page, resets it to the last 15 minutes — repeat card 7.
  • Check the data view is the one the step asks for — auth-* for cards 8 to 12, network-* for cards 13 to 14. If the dropdown is empty or the sidebar shows no fields, re-run the setup file.
  • Check the quotes and the field names. A value containing a dot or a dash must be in double quotes. The fields in this lab are event.code and event.action for the event type — not event.id — plus host.name, user.name, process.name, process.parent.name, source.ip, destination.ip, destination.port and the dns.* fields.

The number in the tab is not what the guide says

  • Are you on the right tab? If you clicked Try ES|QL you are on a different view that caps results at ten and calls the heading “results”. Click Switch to classic. See card 15.
  • Are you reading the tab, or the “Rows per page” line? Only the Documents (N) tab is the total. The table shows at most 100 rows and the ES|QL view shows at most 10.
  • Did the data load twice? Then every count is doubled. The setup script refuses to import on top of existing data, so this should be impossible — but if you imported the .ndjson files by hand as well, run the setup file with reset.
  • Still wrong? Run the setup file again. Its last stage re-runs all seven investigation queries against the live index and prints the count next to the one this guide promises. If any differs it stops and says so, rather than handing you a lab that would mislead you.

The setup file stops with an error

  • “STOPPED at stage N” names the stage that broke, and the message above it says why. Nothing was deleted. Most first-run problems are fixed by opening Docker Desktop, waiting for Engine running, and running the file again.
  • “Something that is NOT this lab is answering on port 9200” — another Elastic Stack is already running. The script refuses to touch it, which is correct. Stop the other one, or change the ESPORT value at the top of the script.
  • “the auth index holds N documents but this lab ships 271” — a partial load. The script refuses to import on top of it, because that would create duplicates. Run the setup file with reset.
  • “Kibana is installed but the engine is not answering” — Docker Desktop is not running.

The teardown file will not remove the volume

  • Is Docker running? A stopped engine cannot delete containers or volumes. The script tells you so and still cleans the scratch folder; start Docker, wait until it is running, and run it again.
  • Did you move or rename the folder? Every object name comes from the folder name, so a renamed folder means the old names no longer match. The script says it cannot find them, which is the safe outcome.
One last thing that is not a fault at all

If you are in another timezone, your clock times will not match the pictures. That is card 7, it is expected, and your gaps will match exactly. If a Summary column shows an empty value, or three DNS lookups show no address, those are real properties of the data — card 13 explains why.

Moving around

On a phone, swipe the card left or right. On a desktop you can also click the pills under the header to jump anywhere.

How to use the screen pictures

Every picture in this guide is a photograph of the running lab, not a drawing. The numbered circles sit on the exact control they describe. Put your browser and the picture side by side, do the same click, and compare.

On a phone the pictures are wider than the screen. Swipe the picture sideways to see the whole of it.

Saving or printing

The printer button at the top right turns this whole guide into a single PDF with every card in order. The Copy button on each dark query box puts that query on your clipboard so you can paste it straight into Kibana.

The coloured markings

Yellow means a value you must read off your own screen and write down — that is your work. There is deliberately no second colour: nothing in this guide is filled in for you, and no answer is printed anywhere inside it. Your instructor holds the key separately.

Stuck on a step?

Almost every problem in this lab has one of three causes, and all three are on the If it breaks card near the end: the time range reset, the wrong data view, or Docker not running. Go there rather than guessing.
